newsitem.title: USA: Panic buying amid cold forecasts ups U.S. propane.
newsitem.headline: Panic buying amid cold forecasts ups U.S. propane.

text.p: A cold front expected to hit much of the U.S. set off panic buying in U.S. propane markets on Monday, causing the market to overheat in what one analyst said were unwarranted price jumps.
Early Monday, meteorologists were predicting much below normal temperatures to blanket the U.S. Northeast and the Midwest by midweek and possibly last through to mid-January.
But some market watchers say the nearly 15 cent price rise on Monday in the Midwest -- a large U.S. retail market -- was unwarranted given the level of inventories.
Although government reports indicate Midwest stocks lagging behind the normal range, analyst Dan Lipee of Petral Consulting said stocks are not in a crisis situation.

"The movement of product out of primary inventory has been going into the secondary and tertiary storage of retailers," said Lippe, noting only primary stocks are counted in Energy Information Administration data.
Retailers, who came into the market this morning in force, supply the winter heating demand of many rural homes as well as demands by the agricultural sector.

According to Lippe and traders, many retailers did not store up on their winter barrels during the traditional stock building summer months in anticipation of prices easing from what were then unseasonal highs.
Not only must they now continue to build inventories but also supply current demand ahead of the forecast for the artic air mass from Siberia, said Lippe.
Traders have confirmed that many of the buyers out Monday were retailers in the Midwest.
But, Lippe said concerns in the marketplace of inventories being too low, which have helped spark up prices, were unwarrented.

Of the 540,000 barrels per day of propane that left primary storage in the Midwest in November, Lippe estimated that about 23.5 percent, or 128,000 bpd, was shifted into secondary and tertiary inventory.
November 1995 clocked a more traditional average of 4,000 bpd.
"That (November 96 estimate) is thirty times the average shift of product from primary to secondary," said Lippe, noting the weather has not yet been as cold as last year.
"The disappearance of product from primary supply was as high in November as we would expect to see in January, when we have the coldest weather," said Lippe.
Such prices have not been seen since the quick runup in the cold snap of December 1989, when prices jumped amid temporary distribution delays.
"It has not even nearly been as cold so far this year as in December 89 and January 90," said Lippe.
